top_reply.author: @JohnLocke-ug2vy
top_reply.text:
@everything777 you are ultimately just repeating the same thing that was said about literally every technological innovation which made some part of the education process easier. 

Calculators, spellchecks, computers, the internet, etc. With every single new technology you always have this same vector of attack. 

However it’s very uninteresting as you are not considering the broader picture. 

Let’s just grant that the internet worsened recall, calculators worsened mental calculation, and spell checks worsened grammar. 

Is that all those things did? No. The internet removed barriers to knowledge. Calculators allowed people to rapidly calculate, and modern ones have memory which allow you to revisit recent calculations to correct any mistakes. Spellchecks allow people to blaze through writing assignments or emails without having to reread their paper 3 times to catch any grammatical errors.  

I could go on.

So what you should be considering is not if skills are being affected negatively, it’s whether those skills should be maximally emphasized and maintained in the first place. 

To extend an olive branch, AI absolutely can produce the outcomes you fear. However that is not a criticism or failure of the technology, that is a failure of the education system to set up bottlenecks which require students to have a certain level of competence.

If your prompt it in lean, you'll get lean. If you prompt it in latex, you'll get latex. This worlds are not mutually exclusive. Both have already occurred. The math Olympiad results were prompted in lean, and the given lean proofs were hard to read. Most of the research level results were prompted in latex and are easy to read. Lean proofs will be like proofs that a proof exists. I don't think there will be much interest in them beyond that, people will still want proofs with human-centric theory. That's the whole point of math. Many garbled collections of first order logic symbols are "true". We don't care, because we don't relate to them. Human interest guides which propositions we call "math", and it always will.

top_comments.author: @claytoncoffman2951
top_comments.text:
"We expect these LLMs to be excellent explainers" does not mean they are. It makes perfect sense that an LLM could prove any provable theorem. The theorem is true or not whether or not the proof exists, we just don't have the evidence without the proof. The proof itself is created (by people or machines) by a string of symbols identified by some methodology. 

The explanation for it though is not something that exists before the proof exists. Whether not an "explaination" is good is subjective, people can disagree about explanations - they cannot disagree about proofs.. There is every reason to believe that an LLM could not hallucinate a verifiable proof, it could though hallucinate an explanation. Like there is a way to test if a proof is true, there is no way to test if an explanation for a proof is true/adequate/best.
